labour.10.why: Order-minded and corporatist camps treat strikes as a disruption to be minimised (or banned), while socialist feminism sees the strike as a core weapon not to be hedged; technopolitical camps and radical feminism have little stake.

notes.STC: Estado Novo's Estatuto do Trabalho Nacional (1933) outlawed strikes and lockouts outright, so a last-resort-only rule is the mild version: 2.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points subordinate labour conflict to the national vertical syndicate, making strikes illegitimate except in extremis: 2.
notes.SF: Zetkin/Kollontai tradition treats strikes (e.g. women's mass strikes, Bread and Roses) as the main lever of working women; hedging them as last resort is resisted: -1.
notes.HF: Hamilton and the Federalists distrusted combinations of workers and favoured order and contract stability: 2.
notes.SUL: Sultanist regimes repress independent unions; a last-resort rule suits the ruler, though doctrine is only loyalty: 2.

violence.10.why: The item divides religious-tradition camps and individual-liberty camps (who permit clergy to fight) from the Catholic-corporatist camp bound by canon law against clergy bearing arms; most others have no stake.

notes.EUR: Orthodox-imperial memory of warrior monks (Peresvet and Oslyabya at Kulikovo, blessed by Sergius of Radonezh) makes defensive fighting by clergy honourable: 2.
notes.CRA: May's Crypto Anarchist Manifesto and cypherpunk ethos hold that anyone may arm and defend themselves; no class is barred: 2.
notes.STC: Salazar's Catholic Estado Novo upheld canon law (c. 1941/1983 forbidding clerics to bear arms), with clergy as chaplains and not combatants: -1.
notes.NAS: Falange's Catholic-imperial militancy glorified the crusade, yet the Church hierarchy kept clergy from arms; adherents split: 1.
